questions.enonce_markdown:
Two statements $p$ and $q$ are defined as:

$p$: Kelvin will go to Kribi

$q$: Kelvin will visit the seaport

Translate into ordinary English, the statements:

(a) $p \Rightarrow q$

(b) $p \wedge q$

(c) $\sim p \vee \sim q$ (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $\Rightarrow$ means "implies" (if ... then), $\wedge$ means "and", $\vee$ means "or" (inclusive) and $\sim$ means "not".

**(a)** $p \Rightarrow q$: **"If Kelvin goes to Kribi, then he will visit the seaport."**

**(b)** $p \wedge q$: **"Kelvin will go to Kribi and he will visit the seaport."**

**(c)** $\sim p \vee \sim q$: **"Kelvin will not go to Kribi or he will not visit the seaport"** (at least one of the two things does not happen; both may fail).

Remark: by De Morgan's law, $\sim p \vee \sim q \equiv \sim(p \wedge q)$, so (c) also says "It is not the case that Kelvin will both go to Kribi and visit the seaport", i.e. (c) is the negation of (b).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The position vectors of the points $A$, $B$ and $C$ are $2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}$ and $7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$ respectively.

Find

(a) the vector equation of the line $AB$.

(b) the cartesian equation of the plane $ABC$.

(c) the sine of the angle between line $AB$ and plane $ABC$. (8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Position vectors: $\mathbf{a} = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k}$, $\mathbf{c} = 7\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k}$.

**(a)** Direction of $AB$:

$$\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a} = (1-2)\mathbf{i} + (1+1)\mathbf{j} + (-4+3)\mathbf{k} = -\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}.$$

The line through $A$ with this direction is

$$\boxed{\mathbf{r} = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k} + t(-\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}), \qquad t \in \mathbb{R}}$$

(equivalently $\mathbf{r} = 2\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 3\mathbf{k} + \lambda(\mathbf{i} - 2\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{k})$). Check: $t = 1$ gives $\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j} - 4\mathbf{k} = \mathbf{b}$.

**(b)** A normal to the plane is $\mathbf{n} = \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}$, where $\overrightarrow{AC} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a} = 5\mathbf{i} + 3\mathbf{j} + 4\mathbf{k}$:

$$\mathbf{n} = \begin{vmatrix} \mathbf{i} & \mathbf{j} & \mathbf{k} \\ -1 & 2 & -1 \\ 5 & 3 & 4 \end{vmatrix} = \mathbf{i}(8 + 3) - \mathbf{j}(-4 + 5) + \mathbf{k}(-3 - 10) = 11\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 13\mathbf{k}.$$

The plane is $\mathbf{r}\cdot\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n}$ with $\mathbf{a}\cdot\mathbf{n} = 2(11) + (-1)(-1) + (-3)(-13) = 22 + 1 + 39 = 62$:

$$\boxed{11x - y - 13z = 62}$$

Check with the three points: $A$: $22 + 1 + 39 = 62$; $B$: $11 - 1 + 52 = 62$; $C$: $77 - 2 - 13 = 62$. All satisfy the equation.

**(c)** The angle $\theta$ between a line with direction $\mathbf{d}$ and a plane with normal $\mathbf{n}$ satisfies $\sin\theta = \dfrac{|\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n}|}{|\mathbf{d}|\,|\mathbf{n}|}$. With $\mathbf{d} = -\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j} - \mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{n} = 11\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j} - 13\mathbf{k}$:

$$\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{n} = (-1)(11) + (2)(-1) + (-1)(-13) = -11 - 2 + 13 = 0.$$

(Here $|\mathbf{d}| = \sqrt6$ and $|\mathbf{n}| = \sqrt{291}$, both non-zero.) Therefore

$$\boxed{\sin\theta = 0, \qquad \theta = 0^\circ}$$

This is expected: the points $A$ and $B$ both belong to the plane $ABC$, so the line $AB$ **lies in the plane** and makes angle $0$ with it. (The question as printed is degenerate: the answer is $0$ for any three points $A$, $B$, $C$.)
